takeaways: An eccentric load on a bolt, rivet or weld group becomes a direct share P/n (or P/A) plus a moment share proportional to distance from the centroid; the two are added as vectors at the worst point.
A bracket bolted to a column face tilts about its edge: bolt tension grows with distance from that edge and is combined with direct shear by a failure theory.
A fillet weld is checked on its throat, 0.707 times the leg; bending stress and direct shear on the throat are combined as a resultant.
Pins, cotters and rivets are designed one failure mode at a time: tension, shear, crushing and bending; the weakest mode sets the strength and the joint efficiency.
Adhesives are strong in shear and weak in peel, and their shear peaks at the ends of an overlap, so wider joints help more than longer ones.
A power screw is an inclined plane: φ > α makes it self-locking but limits its efficiency to below 50 %, and collar friction can take half the torque.
A helical spring's wire is in torsion: τ = K·8WD/(πd³), δ = 8WD³N<sub>a</sub>/(Gd⁴), and its natural frequency must stay far above the load frequency to avoid surge.
Nested springs share deflection, so load divides as their rates; fluctuating loads are checked with mean and alternating shear against a fatigue line.
A leaf spring is a beam of uniform strength; nipping makes all leaves equally stressed without changing the deflection.
Rubber springs are soft in shear and, when bonded, stiff in compression; soft mounts isolate vibration once the forcing frequency exceeds √2 times the natural frequency.
A flywheel's inertia comes from ΔE = Iω²C<sub>s</sub>, and its rim must survive hoop stress ρv² plus bending between the arms.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for design problems rather than derivations in this unit: a bolted or welded bracket under eccentric load, a knuckle or cotter joint, a screw jack, a helical or concentric spring (often under fluctuating load), a leaf spring with nipping, and a flywheel for an engine or punching press. Expect one long question on joints and one on springs or flywheels, and show every failure check with numbers.

bank.q: Explain how a knuckle joint is designed against each of its failure modes, and illustrate the method by sizing a knuckle joint for an axial pull of 40 kN with σ<sub>t</sub> = 80 MPa, τ = 50 MPa and σ<sub>c</sub> = 90 MPa.
outline: Parts of the joint: rod with eye, rod with fork, pin, collar and taper pin
Failure modes: rod in tension, pin in double shear, pin in bending, eye and fork in tension, shear and crushing
Standard proportions d₁ = d, d₂ = 2d, a = 0.75d, b = 1.25d
Pin bending moment M = (P/2)(b/4 + a/3) with load spread over the eye and fork
Numbers: rod 26 mm, pin 34 mm, eye 60 mm, b = 32.5 mm, a = 19.5 mm
Closing check of every stress against its allowable value
answer: A knuckle joint links two rods that carry a pull and must swing a little, as in a valve rod or a tie bar of a roof truss. One rod ends in a single eye of thickness b; the other ends in a fork of two eyes, each of thickness a. A pin of diameter d₁ passes through all three and is held by a collar and a taper pin. The joint is designed by writing one stress for each way it can fail and making each stress no larger than the allowable value.

answer.text: The failure modes and their equations, with P the pull, d the rod diameter and d₂ the outside diameter of the eye:

head: Part
Failure
Stress
rows: Tension or shear across the hole
Tension or shear across the holes

answer: The bending moment comes from how the load spreads along the pin. The eye presses on the middle of the pin with a load spread uniformly over b, and each fork leg reacts P/2 with a load that grows linearly towards the inside face, so its centroid lies a/3 from that face. The moment at the middle of the pin is then M = (P/2)(b/4 + a/3). Taking the load as point loads would give a larger moment and an oversized pin.

answer.text: Rod diameter from tension:
Standard proportions based on the rod: d₁ = d = 26 mm, d₂ = 2d = 52 mm, a = 0.75d = 19.5 mm, b = 1.25d = 32.5 mm. Check the pin at 26 mm:
The pin fails in bending, not shear, so size it for bending:
Eye diameter. With the larger pin the standard d₂ = 52 mm leaves only 18 mm of metal across the eye: 40 000/(32.5 × 18) = 68.4 MPa, above the 50 MPa allowed in shear. Find d₂ from shear of the eye:
Check the eye and fork at d₁ = 34 mm and d₂ = 60 mm:

answer: The remaining parts follow proportion: the collar is about 1.5d₁ = 51 mm across, and the taper pin is about 0.25d₁ = 8.5 mm, say 8 mm. The rod is often thickened near the eye to about 1.1d = 29 mm so that the change in section does not sit at the highest stress.

Result: rod 26 mm, pin 34 mm, eye outside diameter 60 mm, eye thickness 32.5 mm, fork legs 19.5 mm each. Every stress is within its limit: rod 75.3 MPa in tension (40 000/530.9), pin 75.8 MPa in bending and 22.0 MPa in shear, eye 47.3 MPa, fork 39.4 MPa, crushing at most 36.2 MPa. The lesson of the example is that the pin's bending check decides the joint; a design that stops at shear would use a 26 mm pin stressed to 170 MPa.

bank.q: Derive the shear stress and deflection of a close-coiled helical compression spring, explain the Wahl factor, and explain surge. Check your formulas on a spring with D = 40 mm, d = 5 mm, 10 active coils and W = 200 N (G = 80 000 MPa, ρ = 7850 kg/m³).
outline: Free body of half a coil: the wire carries torque WD/2 and direct shear W
Torsion stress 8WD/(πd³) plus direct shear, giving K<sub>s</sub> = 1 + 0.5/C
Curvature raises the inner-fibre stress: Wahl factor K
Deflection from strain energy or the twist of the wire: δ = 8WD³N<sub>a</sub>/(Gd⁴)
Surge: natural frequency of the coils, f<sub>n</sub> = (d/(2πD²N<sub>a</sub>))√(G/2ρ)
Numbers: C = 8, K = 1.184, τ = 193 MPa, δ = 20.5 mm, f<sub>n</sub> = 112 Hz
answer: Cut the spring across the wire and keep one half. The axial load W acts along the spring axis, a distance D/2 from the wire centre. To keep the cut piece in balance the wire section must carry a torque T = WD/2 and a direct shear force W. In a close-coiled spring the helix angle is small, so the wire behaves as a straight bar in torsion.

answer.text: Torsion of a round bar gives the shear at the surface; the direct shear adds roughly uniformly at W/(πd²/4):
answer.pre:
τ<sub>torsion</sub> = 16T/(πd³) = 16(WD/2)/(πd³) = 8WD/(πd³)
τ<sub>direct</sub> = 4W/(πd²) = (8WD/(πd³)) × (d/2D) = (8WD/(πd³)) × 0.5/C
τ = K<sub>s</sub> × 8WD/(πd³),  K<sub>s</sub> = 1 + 0.5/C,  C = D/d

answer: The two stresses add on the inside of the coil, where the torsion shear and the direct shear point the same way. The wire is also curved: fibres on the inside of the coil are shorter than those on the outside, so the same twist strains them more. Wahl combined the curvature effect and the direct shear into one factor: K = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C, and the design stress is τ = K × 8WD/(πd³). K rises sharply for small C, which is why C is kept between about 4 and 12.

answer.text: Deflection. One length of wire πDN<sub>a</sub> twists through an angle θ = TL/(GJ) with J = πd⁴/32. The load moves through the twist times the arm D/2:
answer.pre:
L = πDN<sub>a</sub>
θ = (WD/2)(πDN<sub>a</sub>)/(G × πd⁴/32) = 16WD²N<sub>a</sub>/(Gd⁴)
δ = θ × D/2 = 8WD³N<sub>a</sub>/(Gd⁴)
k = W/δ = Gd⁴/(8D³N<sub>a</sub>)

answer: The same result follows from strain energy: the work done ½Wδ equals the torsion energy T²L/(2GJ) of the wire, which again gives δ = 8WD³N<sub>a</sub>/(Gd⁴). Direct shear adds very little to the deflection and is ignored.

Surge. A spring has mass spread along its coils, so it can vibrate on its own like a string. When a cam opens and closes a valve at a frequency near the spring's natural frequency, a wave of compression runs up and down the coils, some coils close up while others open, and the stress rises far above the static value. For a spring held between two flat plates the lowest natural frequency is f<sub>n</sub> = (d/(2πD²N<sub>a</sub>))√(G/2ρ), in SI units. It is kept 15 to 20 times the operating frequency; otherwise the designer adds a damper, uses nested springs or picks a stiffer, lighter spring.

answer.text: Check on the given spring:

answer: The direct-shear factor alone would give K<sub>s</sub> = 1.0625 and 173.2 MPa, so curvature adds another 11 % at C = 8. A cam running at 5.6 Hz (336 rpm) is the fastest this spring can serve while keeping f<sub>n</sub> 20 times higher.

Closing check: τ = 193 MPa is well inside the 400 to 600 MPa that spring steels allow, the deflection of 20.5 mm at 200 N gives k = 9.77 N/mm, and the stored energy agrees with ½Wδ, so the formulas are consistent with each other.

bank.q: Describe the ways a riveted joint can fail and define its efficiency. Find the efficiency of a single-riveted lap joint of 12 mm plates with 21 mm rivets at a pitch of 50 mm (σ<sub>t</sub> = 80 MPa, τ = 60 MPa, σ<sub>c</sub> = 120 MPa), and show what pitch would make it stronger.
outline: Failure modes: tearing of the plate between holes, shearing of the rivets, crushing of rivet or plate, tearing at the margin
Strength of one pitch length for each mode
Efficiency: least strength over the strength of the solid plate
Unwin's formula for the rivet size and the 1.5d margin
Numbers: P<sub>t</sub> = 27 840 N, P<sub>s</sub> = 20 782 N, P<sub>c</sub> = 30 240 N, η = 43.3 %
Better pitch where tearing and shearing strengths match: 42.6 mm, η ≈ 50 %
answer: A riveted joint holds plates together with rivets that are closed hot or cold in drilled holes. It is designed on one pitch length p, the repeating strip of plate that contains one rivet in each row. In a lap joint the plates overlap and each rivet is in single shear; in a butt joint with two cover plates each rivet is in double shear.

answer.text: There are four ways a joint can fail, each with its strength over one pitch (t the plate thickness, d the hole diameter, n the rivets per pitch):

head: Mode
What happens
Strength per pitch
rows: The plate breaks across the line of holes
The rivets shear at the faying surface
Rivet or plate yields where they bear
The plate splits in front of the rivet

answer: The margin is not calculated in the usual design: it is made large enough by rule, at least 1.5d from the hole centre to the plate edge, so the first three modes decide. The strength of the solid plate over one pitch is S = p·t·σ<sub>t</sub>, and the efficiency is η = least of (P<sub>t</sub>, P<sub>s</sub>, P<sub>c</sub>)/S. It says how much of the plate's strength the holes and rivets leave.

answer.text: Rivet size. Unwin's formula for plates over 8 mm gives a first size:
answer.pre: d = 6√t = 6√12 = 20.8 mm, so a 21 mm hole is consistent with the rule.

answer.text: Strengths for p = 50 mm, one rivet per pitch:

answer: The joint fails by shearing the rivets. Tearing would need 27 840 N and crushing 30 240 N, so the plate between the holes is stronger than it needs to be: the pitch is too large for this rivet.

answer.text: A better pitch makes tearing and shearing equal, so neither mode wastes material:

answer: The efficiency rises from 43.3 % to 50.3 % with no change of rivet: the joint still fails at 20 782 N per rivet, but that is now compared with a narrower strip of plate. The pitch must also stay above about 2d (42 mm) so the rivet can be closed and the plate between holes is not too narrow. A single-riveted lap joint rarely does better than about 50 to 60 %; double or triple rows, or butt joints whose rivets are in double shear, are used where higher efficiency is needed, and a diamond (lozenge) pattern on a tie bar loses only one hole at the first section.
Closing check: least strength 20 782 N against crushing 30 240 N and tearing 21 120 N at p = 43 mm, efficiency 50.3 %, and the 1.5d margin of 31.5 mm rules out margin tearing.

bank.q: A bracket is fixed to a steel plate by six bolts equally spaced on a 200 mm pitch circle, one bolt on the horizontal line through the centre on the load side. A vertical load of 15 kN acts 300 mm from the centre of the circle, in the plane of the bolts. Find the most heavily loaded bolt and the bolt size for an allowable shear stress of 60 MPa on the shank.
outline: Centroid at the centre of the pitch circle; r = 100 mm for every bolt
Primary shear P/6 = 2500 N, downwards on every bolt
Secondary shear Per/Σr² = 7500 N, square to each radius
Vector sum for each bolt; worst bolt on the load side, 10 000 N
Shank area 166.7 mm², d = 14.6 mm, choose M16 at 49.7 MPa
Effect of turning the pattern by 30°
answer: The load is eccentric to the bolt group, so move it to the centroid G of the group, at the centre of the pitch circle, and add the moment it makes there. The bracket then carries a direct load P at G and a moment M = P·e about G. The direct load is shared equally; the moment makes the bracket try to turn about G, and each bolt resists in proportion to its distance from G.

answer.text: Primary and secondary shear:
answer.pre:
P₁ = P/n = 15 000/6 = 2500 N on every bolt, downwards
M = 15 000 × 300 = 4.5 × 10⁶ N·mm, clockwise
r = 100 mm for every bolt, Σr² = 6 × 100² = 60 000 mm²
P₂ = M·r/Σr² = 4.5 × 10⁶ × 100/60 000 = 7500 N, square to each radius

answer: Place G at the origin with x to the right (towards the load) and y upwards. The bolts sit at 0°, 60°, 120°, 180°, 240° and 300°. A clockwise moment pushes each bolt along the clockwise tangent: at (x, y) this direction is (y, −x)/r. Add P₁ = (0, −2500) N to the secondary force of each bolt.

answer.text: Bolt loads:

answer: The bolt at 0°, nearest the load, is the worst because its secondary shear points straight down, in the same direction as the primary shear, so the two add directly: 2500 + 7500 = 10 000 N. The bolt on the far side gets the difference, 5000 N.

answer.text: Size the bolt on its shank, which sits in the shear plane:
If the pattern were turned by 30°, so that no bolt lay on the horizontal line, the worst bolt would sit 30° above the line and its secondary force would be 30° off the vertical:

answer: That is only 2.5 % less, so the bolt size does not change; but it shows that the worst bolt is always the one whose tangent lines up most closely with the load. When the shank is not in the shear plane, the thread core area would be used instead and a larger bolt would follow.

Closing check: the six resultants add as vectors to the full 15 000 N downwards (the horizontal parts cancel in pairs, and the vertical parts sum to −10 000 − 2 × 6250 + 2 × 1250 + 5000 = −15 000 N), and the worst bolt carries 10 000 N at 49.7 MPa in an M16 shank.

bank.q: A bracket is bolted to the face of a steel column by six bolts in three rows of two, at 50 mm, 150 mm and 250 mm above the tilting edge. A load of 25 kN hangs 200 mm from the column face. The allowable tensile stress of the bolts is 80 MPa. Find the bolt size by the maximum principal stress theory and check the maximum shear stress against 40 MPa.
outline: The load makes the bracket tilt about its lower edge; bolt tension is proportional to distance from that edge
Σl² = 175 000 mm²; top-row tension W = Pel/Σl² = 7143 N
Direct shear P/6 = 4167 N on every bolt
Equivalent tension P<sub>e</sub> = ½[W + √(W² + 4P<sub>s</sub>²)] = 9059 N
Stress area 113.2 mm²; choose M16 (157 mm²), 57.7 MPa
Maximum shear 35.0 MPa ≤ 40 MPa
answer: The load P hangs off the column face, so it does two things to the bolts. Its line of action passes the bolt plane, so it shears every bolt equally. Its moment P·e about the column face tries to turn the bracket about its bottom edge, which pulls on the bolts. The bracket is taken as rigid and the bolts as equal springs, so each bolt stretches in proportion to its distance l from the tilting edge and carries a tension proportional to l.

answer.text: The moment balance about the tilting edge, with w the tension per unit distance, is P·e = Σ(w·l)·l = w·Σl², so the tension in any bolt is W = P·e·l/Σl². With two bolts in each row:
Bolt tensions in each row:

answer: The top bolts are the farthest from the tilting edge and carry the most tension: W = 7143 N. Check: 2 × (1429 × 50 + 4286 × 150 + 7143 × 250) = 5.0 × 10⁶ N·mm = P·e.

answer.text: Direct shear and the principal-stress combination. The bolt carries tension W and shear P<sub>s</sub> together, so combine them as stresses on the same area:
Bolt size from the stress area:
answer.pre:
A<sub>s</sub> = P<sub>e</sub>/σ<sub>t</sub> = 9059/80 = 113.2 mm²
M14 (second-choice size): A<sub>s</sub> = 115 mm², σ = 78.8 MPa, almost no margin
M16 (preferred size):    A<sub>s</sub> = 157 mm², σ = 9059/157 = 57.7 MPa ≤ 80 MPa

answer: Choose M16. M14 would pass by 1.5 %, but it is a second-choice size and leaves no room for the preload that the bolt receives when it is tightened.

answer.text: Check by the maximum shear stress theory:
answer.pre:
Equivalent shear force = ½√(W² + 4P<sub>s</sub>²) = ½ × 10 976 = 5488 N
τ<sub>max</sub> = 5488/157 = 35.0 MPa ≤ 40 MPa

answer: Both theories accept M16. Note two points that students often miss: the distance l is measured from the tilting edge, not from the centroid of the bolts; and the direct shear is shared by all six bolts, while the tension is largest only in the top row, so only the top row needs the combined check.

Result: six M16 bolts. The top row carries 7143 N tension and 4167 N shear, giving an equivalent tension of 9059 N, a principal stress of 57.7 MPa against 80 MPa and a maximum shear stress of 35.0 MPa against 40 MPa.

bank.q: A plate bracket is lapped over a column flange and welded to it by two horizontal fillet welds, each 120 mm long, along its top and bottom edges, which are 150 mm apart. A vertical load of 25 kN acts in the plane of the plate, 250 mm from the column end of the welds. The permissible shear stress in the weld is 90 MPa. Find the leg size.
outline: Weld group of two lines; centroid 60 mm from the column end, e = 190 mm
Throat area 169.7h mm², primary shear 147.3/h
Unit polar moment J<sub>u</sub> = 1 638 000 mm³, J = 0.707h·J<sub>u</sub>
Secondary shear at the far ends: components 307.6/h and 246.1/h
Resultant 499.4/h; h = 5.55 mm, take 6 mm, τ = 83.2 MPa
answer: The welds are loaded in their own plane by a load that does not pass through the centroid of the weld group. As with a bolt group, move the load to the centroid and add a twisting moment. Treat each weld as a line of throat thickness 0.707h; the primary shear is shared over the total throat area, and the secondary shear at any point is T·r/J, square to the radius from the centroid.

answer.text: Centroid and eccentricity. Both welds run from the column end (x = 0) to x = 120 mm, at y = ±75 mm:
answer.pre:
Centroid G: x = 60 mm, y = 0
e = 250 − 60 = 190 mm
T = 25 000 × 190 = 4.75 × 10⁶ N·mm, clockwise

answer.text: Throat area and primary shear:
Polar moment of the weld lines about G. For each line of length L at distance y from G, the unit value is L³/12 + L·y²:
Secondary shear at the far ends (60, ±75) mm from G, where the radius is largest and the moment's vertical part adds to the load:
Add the two shears as vectors:

answer: The far ends of both welds are the critical points: there the secondary shear has a downward part that adds to the direct shear. At the column ends the two partly cancel.

answer.text: Leg size:

answer: A 6 mm weld is also a sensible size for plates of 10 to 20 mm, since a much smaller fillet would cool too quickly on thick plate and crack. If the welds were made longer, J would rise roughly as the cube of the length and the leg could be smaller; if they were placed farther apart, the y² term would grow and do the same.

Closing check: the direct shear alone would need only 147.3/90 = 1.6 mm, so the moment, not the load itself, sets the weld. The final weld is 6 mm on both edges, stressed to 83.2 MPa at the far ends and 53.9 MPa at the column ends.

bank.q: Design the screw and nut of a screw jack to lift 40 kN using a single-start square thread 40 mm × 7 mm. Thread and collar friction are both μ = 0.12; the collar has outer and inner radii 32 mm and 18 mm (uniform wear). The screw may be stressed to 80 MPa in compression; the nut bearing pressure is 15 MPa; the effort at the handle is 400 N. The screw has an unsupported length of 300 mm (one end fixed, one free), E = 207 GPa and S<sub>yt</sub> = 400 MPa. Find the torque, efficiency, stresses in the screw, nut height, handle length and the buckling safety, and say whether the jack self-locks.
outline: Thread geometry: d<sub>m</sub> = 36.5 mm, d<sub>c</sub> = 33 mm, α = 3.49°, φ = 6.84°
Raising torque 133.1 N·m, collar torque 120.0 N·m, total 253.1 N·m
Efficiency 17.6 % overall, 33.5 % for the screw alone
Core stresses: 46.8 MPa compression, 18.9 MPa torsion, 30.0 MPa maximum shear
Nut: 7 threads, 49 mm high, 14.2 MPa bearing; thread shear 15.7 and 13.0 MPa
Handle 633 mm; buckling by Johnson: 253.5 kN, factor of safety 6.3
Self-locking: φ > α, lowering torque +42.7 N·m
answer: A screw jack turns a small effort on a long handle into a large lifting force through the inclined plane of the thread. The design checks the torque and efficiency, the stresses in the screw body, the bearing and shear of the nut threads, the handle, and buckling of the screw, and confirms that the load cannot run down on its own.

answer.text: Thread geometry for a square thread 40 × 7:
answer.pre:
d<sub>m</sub> = d − p/2 = 40 − 3.5 = 36.5 mm
d<sub>c</sub> = d − p = 40 − 7 = 33 mm
tan α = l/(πd<sub>m</sub>) = 7/(π × 36.5) = 0.0610, α = 3.49°
tan φ = μ = 0.12, φ = 6.84°
Compression alone needs d<sub>c</sub> ≥ √(4 × 40 000/(π × 80)) = 25.2 mm, so 33 mm is ample.

answer.text: Torque to raise the load:
Efficiency:

answer: The collar takes almost half the torque. A thrust ball bearing under the cup would remove most of it and nearly double the efficiency.

answer.text: Stresses in the screw body between the nut and the head. It carries the load in compression and the thread torque T<sub>r</sub> in torsion (the collar torque is taken at the head):

answer: All three are far below what a screw of 400 MPa yield strength can carry, so the screw body is safe.

answer.text: Nut. Thread depth h = p/2 = 3.5 mm. The number of threads in contact comes from the bearing pressure:
answer.pre:
z = W/(πd<sub>m</sub>·h·p<sub>b</sub>) = 40 000/(π × 36.5 × 3.5 × 15) = 6.64; take z = 7
Nut height H = z·p = 7 × 7 = 49 mm
p<sub>b</sub> = 40 000/(π × 36.5 × 3.5 × 7) = 14.2 MPa ≤ 15 MPa
Screw thread shear: W/(πd<sub>c</sub>·(p/2)·z) = 40 000/(π × 33 × 3.5 × 7) = 15.7 MPa
Nut thread shear:   W/(πd·(p/2)·z) = 40 000/(π × 40 × 3.5 × 7) = 13.0 MPa

answer.text: Handle:
Buckling. One end fixed and one free gives an effective length of 2 × 300 = 600 mm. The radius of gyration of the core is d<sub>c</sub>/4:
answer.pre:
k = 33/4 = 8.25 mm, slenderness = 600/8.25 = 72.7
Limit for Euler = √(2π²E/S<sub>yt</sub>) = √(2π² × 207 000/400) = 101.1
72.7 < 101.1, so use Johnson's formula:
P<sub>cr</sub> = A·S<sub>yt</sub>[1 − S<sub>yt</sub>(L<sub>e</sub>/k)²/(4π²E)]
     = 855.3 × 400 × [1 − 400 × 72.7²/(4π² × 207 000)]
     = 253.5 kN
Factor of safety = 253.5/40 = 6.3

answer: Euler's formula would give 330 kN here, an overestimate, because the screw is too short for elastic buckling to govern.

answer.text: Self-locking:
answer.pre:
φ = 6.84° > α = 3.49°: the jack self-locks.
T<sub>l</sub> = (Wd<sub>m</sub>/2)(μ − tan α)/(1 + μ tan α) = 730 000 × 0.0585 = 42 724 N·mm = +42.7 N·m

answer: The lowering torque is positive, so an effort is needed to lower the load even before the collar friction is counted; the load will not run down by itself. This is also why the screw efficiency is below 50 %.

answer.text: Summary of the design:

head: Item
Value
rows: σ<sub>c</sub> 46.8 MPa, τ 18.9 MPa, τ<sub>max</sub> 30.0 MPa

bank.q: Design a helical compression spring (squared and ground ends) for a cam follower that works between 300 N and 900 N with a stroke of 15 mm. Take C = 6, a factor of safety of 1.5, S<sub>ut</sub> = 1400 MPa, torsional endurance limit S<sub>se</sub> = 310 MPa, G = 81 370 MPa and ρ = 7850 kg/m³. Use the Goodman line with K<sub>s</sub> on the mean stress and K on the alternating stress.
outline: Mean and alternating loads: 600 N and 300 N; rate 40 N/mm
Stress factors K = 1.2525, K<sub>s</sub> = 1.0833
Goodman line gives d = 6.61 mm; choose 7 mm, D = 42 mm
Stresses 202.7 MPa mean, 117.2 MPa alternating, factor of safety 1.68
Coils: N<sub>a</sub> = 8, N<sub>t</sub> = 10; L<sub>s</sub> = 70 mm, L<sub>f</sub> = 96 mm, pitch 10.67 mm
Surge frequency 180 Hz; buckling check L<sub>f</sub>/D = 2.3
answer: The spring sees a load that rises and falls once per cam turn, so it fails by fatigue, not by a single overload. Split the load into a steady mean part and an alternating part, find the two stresses, and size the wire so that the point (τ<sub>m</sub>, τ<sub>a</sub>) lies inside the Goodman line with a factor of safety of 1.5.

answer.text: Loads, rate and stress factors:
Wire diameter. With D = Cd, each stress is τ = (factor) × 8PC/(πd²). Put both into the Goodman line τ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>se</sub> + τ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>su</sub> = 1/n:
Stresses and factor of safety with d = 7 mm. The common factor is 8D/(πd³) = 8 × 42/(π × 7³) = 0.3118 per newton:

answer: A 6 mm wire would give n = 1.24, below the required 1.5, so 7 mm is the smallest wire that works. The peak stress at 900 N, with K on the whole load, is 1.2525 × 900 × 0.3118 = 351.5 MPa, well below the torsional yield strength of about 0.45 × 1400 = 630 MPa, so the spring does not take a set.

answer.text: Active coils for k = 40 N/mm:

answer: With 8 coils the stroke is 14.6 mm, 3 % short of 15 mm. If the full 15 mm is needed, take 8.25 active coils, which wire makers can wind, and the rate falls to 40 N/mm; the stresses do not change because they depend only on load.

answer.text: Lengths with squared and ground ends (two inactive coils):
answer.pre:
N<sub>t</sub> = 8 + 2 = 10
L<sub>s</sub> = N<sub>t</sub>·d = 10 × 7 = 70 mm
L<sub>f</sub> = L<sub>s</sub> + δ<sub>max</sub> + 0.15δ<sub>max</sub> = 70 + 21.84 + 3.28 = 95.1 mm; take 96 mm
Pitch = L<sub>f</sub>/(N<sub>t</sub> − 1) = 96/9 = 10.67 mm
L<sub>f</sub>/D = 96/42 = 2.3 < 4, so no buckling guide is needed

answer.text: Surge check:

answer: The cam may run up to 180/15 = 12 Hz, that is 720 rpm, before the 15-times margin is lost; at higher speeds a stiffer, lighter spring or a nested pair would be needed.

Value
rows: 8 active, 10 total, squared and ground ends

bank.q: Design two concentric helical springs of the same material, free length and solid length to carry a total load of 6 kN with a deflection of about 50 mm. Take C = 7 for both, permissible shear stress 550 MPa and G = 81 370 MPa.
outline: Equal stress and index give P₁/P₂ = (d₁/d₂)² and d₁/d₂ = C/(C − 2) = 1.4
Outer wire from stress: 12.5 mm; choose 14 mm so the inner is a standard 10 mm
D₁ = 98 mm, D₂ = 70 mm, clearance 2 mm
Coils: 5 outer and 7 inner, equal active solid length 70 mm
Rates 83.0 and 42.4 N/mm, deflection 47.9 mm, stresses 438 MPa
answer: Nested springs of the same free length are compressed by the same amount, so they act in parallel: their rates add and the load divides in the ratio of the rates. The usual design makes both springs of the same material with the same index and the same maximum stress. Since τ = K·8PC/(πd²), the same K and C mean that each spring's load is proportional to d².

answer.text: Load sharing. The radial clearance is taken as (d₁ − d₂)/2; writing it as (D₁ − d₁)/2 − (D₂ + d₂)/2 with D = Cd gives the wire ratio:
Outer wire from the stress limit:

answer: The inner wire must be d₁/1.4. A 13 mm outer wire would need a 9.29 mm inner wire, which is not a standard size, while 14 mm gives exactly 10 mm. Choose d₁ = 14 mm and d₂ = 10 mm.

answer.text: Coil diameters, clearance and stresses:

answer: Both springs carry the same stress, 438 MPa, below the 550 MPa allowed: the larger standard wire gives some margin.

answer.text: Active coils for a deflection of 50 mm:
answer.pre:
N₁ = Gd₁⁴δ/(8P₁D₁³) = 81 370 × 14⁴ × 50/(8 × 3973 × 98³) = 5.22; take 5
N₂ = Gd₂⁴δ/(8P₂D₂³) = 81 370 × 10⁴ × 50/(8 × 2027 × 70³) = 7.31; take 7
Active solid lengths: N₁d₁ = 5 × 14 = 70 mm,  N₂d₂ = 7 × 10 = 70 mm

answer: The rounded numbers keep the active solid lengths equal, which is the condition the design asked for.

answer.text: Rates and the actual deflection and load split:

answer: The rounded coil numbers happen to keep the rate ratio at exactly 1.96, so the loads are those planned. With two squared and ground end coils each, the total solid lengths are 7 × 14 = 98 mm and 9 × 10 = 90 mm; the outer spring reaches solid first, so the free length is set from the outer spring: L<sub>f</sub> = 98 + 47.85 × 1.15 = 153 mm for both.
The springs are wound in opposite hands so that the coils of one cannot slip between the coils of the other.

Result: outer spring 14 mm wire on 98 mm mean diameter with 5 active coils, carrying 3973 N; inner spring 10 mm wire on 70 mm with 7 active coils, carrying 2027 N; radial clearance 2 mm; deflection 47.9 mm under 6 kN; both stressed to 438 MPa.

bank.q: A semi-elliptic leaf spring for a truck has an eye-to-eye span of 1100 mm and a central band 100 mm wide. It carries a central load of 12 kN. The leaves are 60 mm × 8 mm, with two full-length leaves including the master leaf; E = 207 000 MPa and the permissible stress is 400 MPa. Find the number of leaves, the stresses with and without nipping, the deflection, the nip and the initial bolt load.
outline: Effective length 2L = 1100 − 100 = 1000 mm, L = 500 mm; load at each eye 6000 N
Number of leaves from the equalised stress 6WL/(nbt²): 11.7, take 12 (2 full-length, 10 graduated)
Without nipping: full-length 540.9 MPa, graduated 360.6 MPa
With nipping: 390.6 MPa in every leaf
Deflection 54.4 mm; nip 19.7 mm; bolt load 769 N
answer: A semi-elliptic spring with a central load 2W acts as two cantilevers, each of length L, loaded by W at the eye. The centre band clamps part of the spring so that it does not bend; the effective length is the span less the band width. The spring will be nipped, so every leaf is designed to the same stress.

answer.text: Effective length and load:
Number of leaves from the equalised stress σ = 6WL/(nbt²):
Stresses if the leaves were not nipped. The full-length leaves then carry 50 % more stress than the graduated leaves:

answer: Without nipping the master leaf would be stressed to 540.9 MPa, 35 % above the 400 MPa allowed, while the graduated leaves would be under-used at 360.6 MPa. Nipping moves stress from the full-length leaves to the graduated ones until all carry 390.6 MPa, which is why it is used on vehicle springs.

answer.text: Deflection at the eye (unchanged by nipping):
Nip and initial bolt load:

answer: The centre bolt must pull the leaves together with 769 N to close the 19.7 mm gap at the ends of the full-length leaves before the spring is fitted.

answer.text: Summary:

head: Item
Value
rows: 12 (2 full-length including the master leaf, 10 graduated), 60 × 8 mm

answer: Closing check: the equalised stress lies between the two unequal stresses (360.6 < 390.6 < 540.9 MPa), as it must, and 2 × 540.9 + 10 × 360.6 = 4688 equals 12 × 390.6 = 4687 to rounding: nipping shares the same total bending between the leaves. The leaf width is 7.5 times the thickness, inside the usual range of 6 to 12.

bank.q: A punching press makes 20 holes a minute, each 25 mm in diameter in plate 18 mm thick of ultimate shear strength 300 MPa. The punching takes one-eighth of each cycle. The flywheel runs at a mean speed of 250 rpm with a total speed variation of 8 %, and its rim has a mean radius of 0.5 m. The rim is cast iron of density 7200 kg/m³, with a width twice its thickness. Find the energy per hole, the flywheel's maximum fluctuation of energy, the rim mass and cross-section, the rim stress and the motor power.
outline: Peak force π·d·t·τ<sub>u</sub> = 424.1 kN; energy per hole ½Ft = 3817 J
Flywheel supplies the punch energy less what the motor gives during the punch: ΔE = 3340 J
Rim speed 13.09 m/s; mass ΔE/(v²C<sub>s</sub>) = 243.7 kg
Section 10 772 mm²; take 150 mm × 75 mm
Hoop stress ρv² = 1.23 MPa; motor power 1.27 kW
answer: The motor of a press is sized for the average power, not the peak. During the short punching stroke the work needed is far more than the motor can supply, so the flywheel gives up part of its kinetic energy and slows down; during the rest of the cycle the motor speeds it up again. The flywheel is sized so that the drop in speed stays within the allowed 8 %.

answer.text: Force and energy per hole. The shearing force is greatest at the start and falls roughly linearly to zero as the punch goes through the plate:
Energy the flywheel must supply. The motor delivers E evenly over each cycle, so during the punch (one-eighth of the cycle) it supplies only one-eighth of E:
Speeds and rim velocity:
Rim mass. For a rim, I ≈ mR², so ΔE = Iω²C<sub>s</sub> = mv²C<sub>s</sub>; the arms and hub are neglected:
Rim cross-section. The rim is a ring of mean circumference 2πR:

answer: The rounded rim is 4.4 % heavier, so the speed variation falls a little to 0.08 × 243.7/254.5 = 0.077, inside the 8 % allowed.

answer.text: Rim stress:

answer: This is tiny, because the rim speed is only 13 m/s, far below the 30 to 40 m/s usually allowed for cast iron. A press flywheel is limited by the energy it must store, not by its strength.

answer.text: Motor power. The motor must supply one hole's energy every 3 s (20 holes a minute):

answer: Without the flywheel the motor would have to deliver 3817 J during one-eighth of 3 s, that is 3817/0.375 = 10.2 kW, eight times as much.

answer.text: Summary:

bank.q: A 300 kg machine running at 1500 rpm is to stand on four rubber mounts loaded in shear, each with a square rubber layer 25 mm thick and G = 0.6 MPa. Not more than 10 % of the shaking force may reach the floor. Find the largest allowable mount stiffness and pad size, choose a pad, and check its natural frequency, transmissibility, static deflection and shear strain.
outline: Transmissibility T = 1/(r² − 1) ≤ 0.10 gives r ≥ √11 = 3.317
Forcing 25 Hz, so f<sub>n</sub> ≤ 7.54 Hz and total k ≤ 672.9 kN/m
Per mount k ≤ 168.2 N/mm; area ≤ 7010 mm², side ≤ 83.7 mm
Choose 80 mm × 80 mm: 153.6 N/mm per mount
Check: f<sub>n</sub> = 7.20 Hz, r = 3.47, T = 0.091, δ<sub>s</sub> = 4.79 mm, γ = 0.19
answer: Isolation needs soft mounts: the forcing frequency must be well above the natural frequency of the machine on its mounts. With little damping the fraction of force transmitted is T = 1/(r² − 1), where r = f/f<sub>n</sub>. Work backwards from the 10 % limit to the largest stiffness, then size the rubber from k = GA/h.

answer.text: Required frequency ratio:
Largest natural frequency and stiffness:
answer.pre:
f = 1500/60 = 25 Hz
f<sub>n</sub> ≤ 25/3.317 = 7.54 Hz
k = m(2πf<sub>n</sub>)² ≤ 300 × (2π × 7.54)² = 672 900 N/m for all four mounts
Per mount ≤ 672 900/4 = 168 200 N/m = 168.2 N/mm

answer.text: Largest pad area from k = GA/h:
answer.pre:
A ≤ k·h/G = 168.2 × 25/0.6 = 7010 mm²
Side of a square pad ≤ √7010 = 83.7 mm

answer: Choose a pad 80 mm × 80 mm, which is a little softer than the limit and so isolates a little better.

answer.text: Check the chosen pad:
Static deflection, strain and stress under the machine's weight:
answer.pre:
Weight per mount = 300 × 9.81/4 = 735.8 N
δ<sub>s</sub> = 735.8/153.6 = 4.79 mm
Check: f<sub>n</sub> = (1/2π)√(9.81/0.00479) = 7.20 Hz, the same
Shear strain γ = 4.79/25 = 0.19
Shear stress τ = 735.8/6400 = 0.115 MPa

answer: The shear strain of 0.19 is moderate: rubber in shear is usually kept below about 0.5 under steady load so that creep stays small. The shear stress of 0.115 MPa is very low because rubber is so soft; the design is set by stiffness, not strength.

answer.text: Results for the chosen mounts:

answer: Two practical points complete the design. The machine passes through 7.2 Hz (432 rpm) every time it starts and stops; rubber's own damping keeps the motion limited during that short passage. The mounts must also hold the machine sideways, so they are often set at an angle or paired with a compression pad that is far stiffer, as a bonded pad with a large shape factor is.
Result: four mounts with 80 mm × 80 mm × 25 mm rubber layers, total stiffness 614.4 N/mm, natural frequency 7.20 Hz and 9.1 % of the shaking force passed to the floor.

bank.q: A bracket carries a vertical load of 12 kN at 250 mm from the centroid of its joint. It can be held either by four bolts at (±50, ±100) mm, allowable shear 60 MPa, or by two vertical fillet welds 200 mm long and 100 mm apart, permissible shear 80 MPa. Size both joints and compare them.
outline: Same method for both: direct share plus moment share, added as vectors at the worst point
Bolts: 3000 N direct, 6708 N moment, worst 8485 N; M16 at 42.2 MPa
Welds: 42.4/h direct, 225.5/h resultant at the top and bottom of the far line; h = 3 mm at 75.2 MPa
Compare material, strength, stiffness, cost, inspection, fatigue and dismantling
Conclusion: when each is the better choice
answer: Both joints are loaded in their own plane by an eccentric load, and both are solved the same way: move the load to the centroid of the group, share the direct load uniformly, share the moment in proportion to the distance from the centroid, and add the two at the worst point. The difference is only that the bolt group is a set of points and the weld group a set of lines.

answer.text: Bolted joint:
Welded joint, with the weld lines at x = ±50 mm, each 200 mm long:
Comparison of the two designs:

head: Aspect
Four M16 bolts
Two 3 mm fillet welds
rows: 225.5 N/mm per mm of leg, 75.2 MPa
Four holes weaken the bracket and column
Can slip if preload is low
Needs a skilled welder and inspection

answer: The welded joint uses its allowable stress far better: every millimetre of weld shares the load, while four discrete bolts must be rounded up to a standard size. The weld adds very little weight and needs no holes. But 3 mm is the smallest fillet that is normally laid, and on plates thicker than about 10 mm a larger fillet is used anyway, because a small weld on a thick plate cools fast and cracks. The weld size is therefore set partly by practice, not only by stress.

The bolts win where the bracket must be taken off for maintenance, where it is fitted on site without welding equipment, or where the column material is hard to weld, such as cast iron. Bolts also make inspection easy: a torque wrench confirms the joint, while a weld needs visual and sometimes ultrasonic checks.

A further difference is the load path under a reversed or vibrating load. Preloaded bolts carry the shear by friction between the plates and see little change in stress; a fillet weld sees the full range at its toes, which concentrate stress, so a welded bracket under vibration may need a larger fillet or a ground toe.

Conclusion: for a bracket that is made once in a workshop and never removed, the welded joint is lighter, stiffer and fully used at 75.2 MPa against 80 MPa. For a bracket that must be removable, fitted on site, or attached to a material that cannot be welded, four M16 bolts at 42.2 MPa against 60 MPa are the better choice, at the cost of four holes and some extra weight.

bank.q: A workshop builds a screw jack for 50 kN with a two-start square thread 50 mm × 8 mm (d<sub>m</sub> = 46 mm), to lift faster, and a nut with only 3 threads engaged. Thread and collar friction are μ = 0.10 and the collar mean radius is 30 mm. Users report that the load creeps down when the jack is shaken and the nut wears quickly. Evaluate the design and recommend changes, with numbers.
outline: Two-start lead 16 mm: α = 6.32° > φ = 5.71°, so the thread overhauls
Thread lowering torque −12.2 N·m; only collar friction holds the load, and vibration releases it
Bearing pressure with 3 threads: 28.8 MPa, above the usual 15 to 18 MPa
Single start: α = 3.17°, lowering torque +51.1 N·m, self-locking
Cost: efficiency 32.2 % falls to 19.3 %, raising torque 395 N·m falls to 330 N·m, twice the turns
Nut with 6 threads (48 mm): 14.4 MPa
answer: Two complaints point to two separate faults: creeping down is a self-locking problem of the thread, and fast wear is a bearing-pressure problem of the nut. Check each with numbers, then compare a single-start thread and a longer nut.

answer.text: Self-locking of the two-start thread:

answer: A negative lowering torque means the load would turn the screw and run down on its own if only the thread friction acted. In this jack the collar friction, T<sub>c</sub> = 0.10 × 50 000 × 30 = 150 N·m, is large enough to hold it while all is still. But vibration lowers the effective friction at the collar (the surfaces slip in small steps), and then the 12.2 N·m tendency of the thread wins. This matches the complaint: the jack is self-locking only by its collar, and that cannot be relied on.

answer.text: Nut bearing pressure with 3 threads (thread depth p/2 = 4 mm):

answer: Permissible bearing pressures for a steel screw in a bronze nut at low rubbing speed are usually 15 to 18 MPa. At 28.8 MPa the oil film is squeezed out and the nut wears fast: the second complaint.

answer.text: Compare the two-start thread with a single-start thread of the same size (lead 8 mm):
The figures come from T<sub>r</sub> = (Wd<sub>m</sub>/2)(μ + tan α)/(1 − μ tan α) and η = Wl/(2πT):

answer: The two-start thread is more efficient, and its screw efficiency of 52 % is itself the warning sign: a screw that is more than 50 % efficient cannot be self-locking. The single-start thread needs twice as many turns, but each turn needs less torque, 330 N·m instead of 395 N·m, so with a 600 mm handle the effort drops from 658 N to 549 N.

answer.text: Nut length for the single-start thread:
answer.pre:
z = 50 000/(π × 46 × 4 × 15) = 5.8; take z = 6
p<sub>b</sub> = 50 000/(π × 46 × 4 × 6) = 14.4 MPa ≤ 15 MPa
Nut height = 6 × 8 = 48 mm (z = 5 would give 17.3 MPa, at the top of the range)

answer: Recommendations: (1) use a single-start thread, so the jack holds its load by the thread itself, with T<sub>l</sub> = +51.1 N·m in hand; (2) lengthen the nut to 6 threads, 48 mm, which halves the bearing pressure to 14.4 MPa; (3) keep the collar plain rather than fitting a thrust bearing: in a lifting device holding the load matters more than a lower effort, and a ball thrust bearing would remove the collar's extra holding torque. If faster lifting is truly needed, a two-start thread could be kept only with a separate brake or ratchet that holds the load, which adds cost and a part that can fail.

Judgement: the two-start design traded safety for speed, and in a lifting device that trade is wrong. The single-start thread with a 48 mm nut is slower and less efficient, 19.3 % against 32.2 %, but it cannot let the load down, and its nut will last.

glossary.def: The axial distance between neighbouring threads.
The axial advance of a screw in one turn: pitch times the number of starts.
For a square thread d<sub>m</sub> = d − p/2; used in the lead angle and the torque.
The angle α of the unwrapped thread: tan α = l/(πd<sub>m</sub>).
φ = tan⁻¹μ; a screw self-locks when φ > α.
A screw lowers its load by itself because φ < α.
The clamping tension put into a bolt when it is tightened.
The weakest section of a fillet weld, 0.707 times the leg.
Shear across two sections at once, as in a knuckle pin or a cotter.
Failure by compressive bearing on a projected area, such as a pin on its hole.
The distance from a rivet centre to the plate edge, usually 1.5d.
A diamond rivet pattern on a tie bar that loses only one hole at the first section.
The concentration of shear at the ends of an adhesive overlap.
C = D/d, mean coil diameter over wire diameter.
The coils that deflect; end coils only seat the spring.
The length of a spring with every coil touching.
Resonance of a spring's coils when the load frequency matches its natural frequency.
Blasting the wire with small shot to leave compressive stress at the surface and raise fatigue strength.
The longest leaf of a leaf spring, rolled into eyes at both ends.
Pre-bending the full-length leaves so that all leaves reach equal stress under load.
For a rubber block, one loaded area divided by the free area that can bulge.
The fraction of a vibrating force that a mount passes to the floor.
C<sub>s</sub> = (ω₁ − ω₂)/ω.
The largest change in the flywheel's stored energy in one cycle, ΔE.
